area: Area VII. Slow Flight and Stalls
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain how angle of attack, airspeed, load factor, power, weight, CG and yaw interact at low speed, and fly coordinated level flight, turns, climbs and descents just above the stall warning within ACS tolerances.
why: Takeoffs, departures, approaches and landings are all flown slow and close to the ground. Knowing how the airplane feels and behaves near the stall warning is what keeps a slow airplane from becoming a stalled one.

prereading.what: Angle of attack, slow flight, the backside of the power curve, performing and exiting the maneuver, common errors.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 5, 5-9 to 5-12

prereading.what: Stall recognition cues, AOA indicators, stall characteristics and the stall recovery template.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 5, 5-13 to 5-16

prereading.what: Factors that change stall speed: load factor, CG, weight, configuration, turbulence; distractions; stall warning cues.
prereading.label: AC 61-67C, pages 1-5 (par 100-105)

prereading.what: Left-turning tendencies: torque, slipstream, gyroscopic action and P-factor.
prereading.label: PHAK 5-31 to 5-32

warmup: Your airspeed is 10 knots above the stall and you roll into a 30° bank without adding power. What happens to your margin above the stall, and why?

key_terms.def: Flying at an airspeed where any more AOA, load factor, or less power would set off the stall warning.
Angle between the wing's chord line and the relative wind.
The AOA where airflow separates and the wing stalls. Can be reached at any airspeed, attitude or power.
Lift divided by weight, in G. Goes up in turns and pull-ups.
Published stall speed. Valid only in level, coordinated flight at one weight and CG.
Speed of minimum drag. Below it, slowing down takes more power, not less.
Speeds below L/DMAX. Pitch controls airspeed, power controls the flightpath.
Nose yawed straight into the relative wind; ball centered.
Buffet, horn, light or stick shaker that warns you near the critical AOA.

body.p: Slow flight is flying at an airspeed where any more AOA, more load factor, or less power will set off the stall warning (buffet, stall horn, etc.) [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. You fly it at a safe altitude so you know the feel, sounds and sight picture you will have on takeoff and landing.
The goal: fly at low speed and high AOA, where controls respond less and altitude is harder to hold [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. You must:

bullets: Understand the aerodynamics in each configuration
Recognize the airplane's cues
Fly coordinated without a stall warning
Correct at once if a stall warning comes on [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]

callout.text: Target: 5 to 10 knots above the 1G stall speed for that configuration [[24:114|AFH 5-9]] [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

body.p: How to find your target speed: in the slow flight configuration, slow to the stall warning, lower the nose slightly until the warning stops, add power to hold altitude, and note the airspeed [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].
Controls feel "sloppy" or "mushy" because less air flows over them. The slower you go, the bigger the control movements you need [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

check.q: What three things will set off the stall warning when you are in slow flight?
check.a: More AOA, more load factor, or less power [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

body.p: A wing stalls when it passes its critical AOA, not because airspeed is low [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. Lift and drag both rise with AOA until the critical AOA, then lift drops [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].
Load factor raises stall speed. Stall speed goes up with the square root of the load factor. Example: a 45-knot stall speed becomes 90 knots at 4 G [[13:8|AC 61-67C p2]].

head: Level coordinated bank
Load factor
Stall speed
rows: 41 percent higher [[24:114|AFH 5-9]] (AC 61-67C rounds to 40 percent [[13:7|AC 61-67C p1]])

body.p: In slow flight you are already close to the stall. A turn adds load factor, so you need more AOA and more power to hold altitude [[24:73|AFH 3-12]] [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. That is why turns in slow flight use smooth, shallow-to-medium banks (climbing turns about 20° [[24:115|AFH 5-10]]).

callout.text: It is possible to stall at any airspeed, in any attitude, at any power setting [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

check.q: An airplane stalls at 45 knots in level flight. About what is its stall speed at 4 G?
check.a: 90 knots. Stall speed rises with the square root of load factor [[13:8|AC 61-67C p2]].

chunks.title: Power and the backside of the power curve

body.p: Above L/DMAX, more power is needed to go faster. Below L/DMAX, more power is needed to go slower [[24:115|AFH 5-10]]. Slow flight is well below L/DMAX, so you need large power inputs or less AOA to stop the airplane from slowing further [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

bullets: Pitch controls airspeed. Power controls the flightpath (climb, level, descent) [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].
Small pitch changes make big changes in induced drag and airspeed [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].
Speed instability: if a gust slows you, airspeed keeps dropping unless you lower AOA or add power [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

body.p: On the backside, a little forward pressure trades a bit of altitude for speed and moves you toward the middle of the curve, where there is excess power to climb or turn [[24:91|AFH 4-5]].

callout.text: As you near target speed you'll need to ADD power to hold altitude [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. This surprises most students.

check.q: In slow flight, which control mainly holds airspeed and which holds altitude?
check.a: Pitch holds airspeed; power holds altitude (the flightpath) [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

head: Factor
Effect
rows: Higher stall speed; needs more AOA for the extra lift [[13:9|AC 61-67C p3]]
Stalls at a higher speed; more back-elevator force [[1:141|PHAK 5-44]]
Less elevator needed to stall, so inadvertent stalls come easier; less stable [[13:8|AC 61-67C p2]] [[1:141|PHAK 5-44]]
Lower stall speed (white arc starts below green arc), more drag [[13:7|AC 61-67C p1]] [[13:8|AC 61-67C p2]]
Higher stall speed; ice can remove the normal cues [[13:9|AC 61-67C p3]] [[13:10|AC 61-67C p4]]

body.p: The published 1G stall speed is only true in unaccelerated 1G flight, coordinated, at one weight (usually max gross) and one CG (usually most forward) [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. Change any of these and your real stall speed changes.

Attitude: slow flight is flown nose-high with high power [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. But pitch attitude alone won't tell you how close you are to a stall, because a stall can happen in any attitude [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

callout.text: Raising flaps abruptly in slow flight can stall the airplane. Anticipate the AOA change [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

check.q: Why does the airplane stall at a higher speed with a forward CG?
check.a: The stalling AOA is reached at a higher speed due to increased wing loading [[1:141|PHAK 5-44]].

body.p: At low airspeed, high AOA and high power, torque, slipstream and P-factor yaw the nose left. Hold right rudder. The closer to the 1G stall, the more right rudder you need [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

bullets: P-factor: at high AOA the down-going (right) blade takes a bigger bite, pulling the nose left [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].
Slipstream: at high power and low speed the spiral is tight and pushes hard on the tail [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].
Adverse yaw: when you roll, the rising wing has more drag and yaws the nose the other way. Use rudder with aileron [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

body.p: Skid: ball to the outside, you feel pushed outward. Slip: ball to the inside, you feel pushed inward [[24:74|AFH 3-13]]. Coordinated means the ball is centered [[24:113|AFH 5-8]].

callout.text: The main cause of an inadvertent spin is exceeding the critical AOA with too much or too little rudder [[13:12|AC 61-67C p6]]. Slow flight is right next to that critical AOA.

body.p: Uncoordinated flight also makes the airspeed indicator and altimeter unreliable, so the stall warning may be your first clue [[13:12|AC 61-67C p6]].

check.q: In slow flight at high power, which rudder do you usually need, and why?
check.a: Right rudder, to counter the left yaw from torque, slipstream and P-factor [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

bullets: 1. Pick an altitude so you finish no lower than 1,500 ft AGL (single-engine), or higher if the manufacturer says so [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].
2. Clear the area. Some programs require two 90° turns in opposite directions [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].
3. Reduce power from cruise. Raise the nose as needed to hold altitude while airspeed drops [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Listen for the change in airflow sound.
4. Configure as the examiner asks. Usually landing configuration: do the before-landing checks; extend flaps (and gear) only below their limit speeds [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].
5. Near target speed (5-10 knots above stall for that configuration), add power to hold altitude [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Trim off the back pressure [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].
6. Hold heading with right rudder, ball centered [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Look outside and cross-check the instruments [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].
7. Turns: add power to hold altitude; keep inputs smooth [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Climbing turns use medium bank, about 20° [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

8. Climbs and descents: from stabilized level slow flight, change power to climb or descend [[24:116|AFH 5-11]], and use pitch to hold the airspeed [[24:115|AFH 5-10]]. Expect more left yaw at high power.
9. Exit: add power, then forward pressure as speed builds to hold altitude. Stay coordinated, level the wings, retract flaps/gear in steps, retrim [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].
10. Stall warning at any time? Lower the AOA first, then level wings and add power [[24:120|AFH 5-15]] [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

body.p: Also on the checkride: clear the area (ACS PA.VII.A.S1); pick an entry altitude so you finish no lower than 1,500 ft AGL (ACS PA.VII.A.S2); hold an airspeed where any more AOA, load factor or power reduction would trigger a stall warning (ACS PA.VII.A.S3); and fly coordinated straight-and-level, turns, climbs and descents in the examiner's configuration with no stall warning (ACS PA.VII.A.S4).

callout.text: Airspeed is +10/-0. Going below target is out of tolerance, and so is any stall warning (ACS PA.VII.A.S4, S5).
Speeds, flap limits and power settings are in your POH/AFM. The AFH gives only generic guidance.

check.q: You are in level slow flight and want to climb 200 feet. What do you move first?
check.a: Add power; pitch keeps the airspeed. Climbs and descents in slow flight are made by adjusting power [[24:116|AFH 5-11]] [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

head: Error [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]
Fix
rows: Too little back pressure as power comes off: altitude loss
Raise the nose as the power comes back
Too much back pressure: climb, then fast speed loss
Keep the ball centered; more rudder as you slow
Mostly look outside; quick instrument cross-checks
Not anticipating AOA change with flaps
Change flaps in steps; adjust pitch as they move
Power for altitude; expect to add power near target and in turns
Practice with simple tasks added, one at a time
Trim off the back pressure at target speed
Not responding to a stall warning

body.p: If you stay trimmed for cruise, you'll need strong back pressure, which makes precise control hard [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

check.q: Name the last common error the AFH lists, and the fix.
check.a: Failure to respond to a stall warning [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]. Fix: reduce the AOA first [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

chunks.title: Risk: stall warnings and inadvertent slow flight

body.p: Inadvertent slow flight is what you are training to catch. A distracted pilot on takeoff, approach or a windy pattern can slide into it without noticing [[13:9|AC 61-67C p3]]. Once at the warning, the next step is a stall and possible loss of control.

head: Warning
Range and limits
rows: Many warn 4 to 8 knots before the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C p4]]. Must not be disabled for a checkride when required equipment [[13:22|AC 61-67C p16]].
Certification allows buffet in place of a device. Most vintage airplanes, and many light-sport and experimental ones, have no device [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].
Mushy controls, quieter airflow, seat-of-the-pants [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. Fixed-pitch prop: RPM may drop near a power-on stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C p4]].
Shows the margin to critical AOA. Limits: calibration, unheated probes, type, flap setting, contamination [[24:118|AFH 5-13]] [[24:119|AFH 5-14]].

bullets: Power-off cues (buffet, shaking) are weaker than power-on [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. Watch this in slow-flight descents.
With ice, a stall may come with little or none of the usual cues [[13:10|AC 61-67C p4]].
Pitch attitude is not a sure cue: you can stall in any attitude [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

callout.text: Any warning = reduce AOA first. Then wings level, then power [[24:120|AFH 5-15]] [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

check.q: About how far ahead of the stall do many stall warning devices activate?
check.a: 4 to 8 knots before the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C p4]].

head: Hazard
Why it bites in slow flight
rows: A vertical gust changes the relative wind and suddenly raises AOA; you can stall at a much higher airspeed [[13:9|AC 61-67C p3]].
Downdrafts up to 6,000 fpm and headwind losses of 30-90 knots [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. Headwind turning to tailwind drops airspeed and performance [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].
Less power, less thrust and less lift [[1:91|PHAK 4-4]], so less power to hold altitude at low speed. Indicated stall speed does not change [[13:9|AC 61-67C p3]].

body.p: Collision: the nose is high and you're busy, so traffic hides. More than one-quarter (26.6 percent) of fatal accidents in 10 years happened in maneuvering flight, and the maneuvering itself distracts from scanning [[16:12|AC 90-48E p12]]. Clear first. Scan in steps of no more than 10°, at least 1 second each [[24:32|AFH 1-11]]. Bank gently left and right to see blind spots [[16:13|AC 90-48E p13]].

Distraction: stalls from poor airspeed control happen most when the pilot is busy with something else: a checklist, a chart, items on the floor [[13:9|AC 61-67C p3]]. Aviate first; look outside and cross-check instruments to stay oriented [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

check.q: Why can turbulence cause a stall at an airspeed well above the published stall speed?
check.a: A vertical gust suddenly changes the relative wind and raises AOA [[13:9|AC 61-67C p3]].

scenario.title: Slow flight on a hot, bumpy afternoon
scenario.setup: You're practicing slow flight solo in a high-wing trainer with full fuel and a bag in back. It's a hot afternoon; the practice area sits 2,000 ft above sea level, and towering cumulus are building to the west. You're in landing configuration at your target speed when the airplane starts bouncing in light turbulence. The radio calls out a traffic alert nearby, and you lean down to find your tablet. When you look up, the ball is out to the right, the nose has drifted left, and the stall horn chirps.

questions.q: The horn chirps. What is your first action?
questions.a: Reduce the AOA (forward pressure) until the warning stops, then level the wings, add power as needed, and stay coordinated [[24:120|AFH 5-15]] [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Not responding to a stall warning is a listed common error [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

questions.q: Why did the bumps make a stall more likely, even at your normal target speed?
questions.a: A vertical gust changes the relative wind and abruptly raises AOA, so you can stall at a higher airspeed [[13:9|AC 61-67C p3]]. Below L/DMAX, a speed loss from a gust keeps getting worse unless you lower AOA or add power [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

questions.q: How did the heavy load and hot day shrink your margin?
questions.a: More weight raises stall speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C p3]]. High density altitude cuts power, thrust and lift [[1:91|PHAK 4-4]], so you have less extra power to hold altitude at low speed.

questions.q: The ball is out and the nose is yawing left. Why does that matter so close to the stall?
questions.a: You were not holding enough right rudder for the left-turning tendencies [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Exceeding the critical AOA while uncoordinated is the main cause of an inadvertent spin [[13:12|AC 61-67C p6]].

questions.q: What about the building cumulus to the west?
questions.a: Microbursts come from convective weather and can produce downdrafts up to 6,000 fpm and big airspeed losses [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. Move the practice away from them, or end the lesson.

questions.q: How should you have handled the traffic call and the tablet?
questions.a: Fly first. Maneuvering flight distracts from scanning [[16:12|AC 90-48E p12]], and stalls from poor airspeed control happen when pilots reach for items or charts [[13:9|AC 61-67C p3]]. Exit slow flight, then look for the traffic outside with a good scan [[24:32|AFH 1-11]].

skills.practice: Two 90° clearing turns in opposite directions, or your CFI's method, every time [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

skills.do: Pick an entry altitude so the whole maneuver ends no lower than 1,500 ft AGL.
skills.practice: Before takeoff, find the highest terrain in your practice area and add 1,500 ft plus a margin [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

skills.do: Hold an airspeed where any more AOA, load factor or power reduction would trigger a stall warning.
skills.practice: Find your target speed for each configuration: slow to the warning, lower the nose until it stops, add power to hold altitude, note the speed [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

skills.do: Fly coordinated straight-and-level, turns, climbs and descents in the examiner's configuration with no stall warning.
skills.practice: Practice in landing, takeoff and clean configurations [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Add simple tasks one at a time (find a heading on the chart, climb 200 ft) [[13:16|AC 61-67C p10]].

skills.do: Hold altitude ±100 ft, heading ±10°, airspeed +10/-0 knots, bank ±10°.
skills.practice: Trim at target speed, then make only small pitch and power changes. Call out altitude, heading and airspeed every few seconds.

options: Airspeed drops below the published stall speed
It exceeds its critical angle of attack
The nose is above the horizon
quiz.why: A stall is the result of exceeding the critical AOA, not low airspeed [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

quiz.q: The AFH's suggested target speed for slow flight is:
options: 5 to 10 knots above the 1G stall speed
quiz.why: 5 to 10 knots above the 1G stall speed is a good target [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

quiz.q: In level slow flight, below L/DMAX, to slow down further while holding altitude you need:
quiz.why: Below L/DMAX, more power is required to fly even slower [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

quiz.q: In a level, coordinated 60° bank, the stall speed is about:
quiz.why: Load factor is 2 G and stall speed is 41 percent higher [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

quiz.q: Close to the stall at high power, a single-engine trainer usually needs:
quiz.why: Torque, slipstream and P-factor yaw the nose left; the closer to the 1G stall, the more right rudder [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

quiz.q: The ACS airspeed tolerance for slow flight is:
Many stall warning devices activate about:
quiz.why: Many devices alert the pilot 4 to 8 knots before the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C p4]].

quiz.q: What is the first action when a stall warning sounds in slow flight?
options: Add full power and hold altitude
quiz.why: The most important action is to reduce the AOA [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. Raising flaps abruptly can cause a stall [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

takeaways: Slow flight = just above the stall warning; any more AOA, G or less power sets it off.
Stalls come from critical AOA, not low airspeed. Turns, weight and forward CG raise stall speed.
Below L/DMAX: pitch for airspeed, power for altitude, and expect to add power.
Hold right rudder and keep the ball centered; uncoordinated near the stall leads to spins.
ACS: altitude ±100 ft, heading ±10°, airspeed +10/-0 knots, bank ±10°, no stall warning.
Any stall warning: reduce AOA first.
cfi_notes: Current guidance and ACS S3/S4 want slow flight WITHOUT a stall warning. AC 61-67C's older stall-avoidance drill ('maintain heading and altitude with the stall warning device activated' [[13:15|AC 61-67C p9]]) predates this; don't teach slow flight on the horn for the checkride.

The task file's objective says 'cruise configuration', but S4 says 'configured as specified by the evaluator' and the AFH says slow flight is typically evaluated in landing configuration [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Train in landing, takeoff and clean.
Have the student find the target speed for each configuration in your airplane, using the AFH method [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].
Use AC 61-67C distraction tasks (drop a pencil, find a heading on a chart, climb 200 ft) once the basic maneuver is solid [[13:16|AC 61-67C p10]].
Demonstrate adverse yaw at low speed: turns without rudder [[13:15|AC 61-67C p9]]. Then release the rudder to show the left yaw.
Watch for fixation on the airspeed indicator and failure to trim [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]. Examiners note whether the applicant clears the area and keeps scanning.
Show how abrupt flap retraction in slow flight costs lift; teach flaps up in steps [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].
gaps: Target speeds, flap and gear limit speeds, power settings and stall warning activation speed are airplane-specific: use the POH/AFM.
The task file's objective says 'cruise configuration' while S4 and the AFH call for the examiner's configuration (usually landing). Confirm the current ACS wording.
The sources give no slow-flight-specific guidance on disorientation; the lesson uses the AFH advice to keep outside references and cross-check instruments.
Sources say high density altitude reduces power, thrust and lift, but don't quantify its effect on slow flight; RMH (FAA-H-8083-2) has no slow-flight-specific content.

activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: More power is needed to go faster
Fast cruise at a low angle of attack
More power is needed to go slower
Small pitch changes make big swings in drag and airspeed
A gust slows you, and the speed keeps dropping unless you act
A little forward pressure trades altitude for speed and extra power

activities.title: What does it do to the stall?
activities.intro: Tap a factor, then what it does near the stall.

pairs.r: Higher stall speed; needs more AOA for the extra lift
Stalls at a higher speed; more back-elevator force
Less elevator needed to stall, so accidental stalls come easier
Lower stall speed and more drag

pairs.l: Frost or ice on the wing
pairs.r: Higher stall speed, and the usual warnings may not come

activities.title: Slow flight from start to finish
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Reduce power from cruise and raise the nose to hold altitude
Below the flap limit speed, extend flaps for landing
Near target speed, add power to hold altitude, then trim
Fly turns, climbs and descents with no stall warning
As speed builds, add forward pressure to hold altitude
Retract flaps in steps and retrim

cards.s: Many stall warning devices sound 4 to 8 knots before the stall.
cards.why: Yes. Many airplanes have devices that warn the pilot 4 to 8 knots before the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C p4]].

cards.s: Every certificated airplane must have a stall horn, light or shaker.
cards.why: No. Certification lets the warning come from natural buffet instead. Most vintage airplanes, and many light-sport and experimental ones, have no device [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

cards.s: Buffet and shaking are usually stronger in a power-off stall than a power-on stall.
cards.why: No. Power-off cues are less noticeable than power-on cues [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. Keep this in mind in slow-flight descents.

cards.s: With ice on the wings, a stall can come with little or no warning.
cards.why: Yes. In some icing conditions the stall may come with little or none of the usual cues [[13:10|AC 61-67C p4]].

cards.s: When the stall horn sounds, add full power and hold altitude first.
cards.why: No. Reduce the AOA first. Pilots who put power and altitude first have lost control [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

cards.s: An AOA indicator can be less accurate if its probe is not heated or the wing is dirty.
cards.why: Yes. Unheated probes or vanes and wing contamination are on the list of AOA indicator limits [[24:119|AFH 5-14]].

final_quiz.q: You are in level slow flight in landing configuration with no stall warning. Which action is most likely to set off the stall warning?
options: Rolling into a 20° bank and holding altitude with back pressure only
final_quiz.why: In slow flight, any more AOA, more load factor, or less power will set off the stall warning [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. A turn adds load factor, so you must add power to hold altitude [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Using back pressure alone raises the AOA.

final_quiz.q: Your trainer's 1G stall speed in landing configuration is 48 knots. Which target airspeed fits the AFH guidance for slow flight?
final_quiz.why: A good target is 5 to 10 knots above the 1G stall speed, here 53 to 58 knots [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. 48 knots is the stall itself, and 70 knots is not slow flight.

final_quiz.q: A trainer stalls at 50 knots in straight-and-level flight. The pilot rolls into a coordinated level turn at 60° of bank. About what is the stall speed now?
final_quiz.why: A level 60° bank is 2 G, and the stall speed is 41 percent higher [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]: 50 × 1.41 is about 71 knots. Stall speed goes up with the square root of load factor, so doubling the G does not double it [[13:8|AC 61-67C p2]].

final_quiz.q: You are holding altitude in slow flight when the airspeed starts sliding below your target. What is the best fix?
options: Raise the nose to hold altitude
Lower the nose slightly and add power to hold altitude
Reduce power to settle the airplane
Raise the flaps quickly to cut drag
final_quiz.why: Below L/DMAX, pitch controls airspeed and power controls the flightpath. Airspeed keeps dropping unless you lower the AOA or add power [[24:115|AFH 5-10]]. Raising the flaps abruptly can stall the airplane [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

final_quiz.q: Look at the power curve. You are at point 3, slow and close to the stall. What does a little forward pressure do?
options: Trades a little altitude for speed and moves you toward point 2, where there is excess power to climb or turn
Slows the airplane further toward the stall line
Raises the power required, so the airplane climbs
Nothing, because only power changes airspeed on the backside
final_quiz.why: On the backside, forward pressure gives a brief descent that speeds the airplane up from 3 toward 2. Drag drops and you gain excess power to climb or turn [[24:91|AFH 4-5]].

final_quiz.q: You fly slow flight twice in the same airplane: once with the CG near the forward limit and once near the aft limit. What is true of the aft CG flight?
options: It stalls at a higher speed than with a forward CG
It takes less elevator to reach the stall, so an accidental stall comes easier
It needs more back-elevator force to hold the nose up
It is the condition the published stall speed is usually based on
final_quiz.why: With an aft CG, less elevator is needed to stall, which makes inadvertent stalls easier [[13:8|AC 61-67C p2]]. A forward CG stalls at a higher speed and needs more back pressure [[1:141|PHAK 5-44]]. The published speed usually assumes the most forward CG [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

final_quiz.q: Your POH stall speed was set at max gross weight and forward CG. In which of these conditions is your real stall speed most likely higher than that number?
options: Flying at 6,500 feet instead of near sea level
On a hot day with high density altitude
Straight and level, ball centered, at max gross weight and forward CG
In a level, coordinated 30° bank turn
final_quiz.why: The published 1G stall speed holds only in unaccelerated, coordinated flight at one weight and one CG [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. A turn adds load factor. Altitude and temperature have little or no effect on indicated stall speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C p3]].

final_quiz.q: In slow flight you add full power to start a climb. The nose yaws left and the ball slides right. What causes it, and what is the fix?
options: Torque, slipstream and P-factor; add right rudder
Adverse yaw from the ailerons; add left rudder
final_quiz.why: At low speed and high power, torque, slipstream and P-factor yaw the nose left, and right rudder keeps you coordinated [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. At high AOA the down-going right blade makes more thrust than the left one [[13:12|AC 61-67C p6]].

final_quiz.q: You are in a slow-flight turn to the left. The ball is out to the right, toward the outside of the turn, and you feel pushed outward. What is happening, and why does it matter?
options: A slip; it is harmless at low speed
A skid; exceeding the critical AOA while uncoordinated is the main cause of inadvertent spins
A slip; add more aileron into the turn
final_quiz.why: Ball to the outside and a push outward mean a skid [[24:74|AFH 3-13]]. Exceeding the critical AOA with too much or too little rudder is the primary cause of an inadvertent spin [[13:12|AC 61-67C p6]].

final_quiz.q: On your checkride the examiner asks for slow flight at 4,500 feet, heading 090°, with a target airspeed of 55 knots. Which reading is within the ACS standard?
final_quiz.why: The ACS allows altitude ±100 feet, heading ±10° and airspeed +10/-0 knots (ACS PA.VII.A.S5). 53 knots is below target, 4,380 feet is 120 feet low, and 103° is 13° off. Slower than target moves you toward the stall warning, which slow flight must avoid [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

final_quiz.q: The highest terrain in your practice area is 1,300 feet MSL. You want to finish slow flight no lower than 1,500 feet AGL, even if you drift 100 feet low. What is the lowest of these entry altitudes that works?
final_quiz.why: 1,300 + 1,500 = 2,800 feet MSL, plus 100 feet of margin is 2,900. Slow flight in a single-engine airplane should end no lower than 1,500 feet AGL [[24:115|AFH 5-10]]. 3,500 also works but is not the lowest.

final_quiz.q: You finish slow flight with full flaps. You add full power and raise all the flaps at once. What is the main risk?
options: Nothing, because full power is in
A sudden loss of lift that can stall the airplane
final_quiz.why: Abruptly raising the flaps in slow flight can stall the airplane, so anticipate the AOA change and retract them in steps as speed builds [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

final_quiz.q: You are practicing slow flight on a gusty afternoon at your normal target speed. Why is your stall margin smaller than the airspeed indicator suggests?
options: A vertical gust can suddenly raise the AOA and stall the wing at a higher airspeed
Gusts make the airspeed indicator read too low
final_quiz.why: A vertical gust changes the relative wind and abruptly raises the AOA, so the airplane can stall at a much higher airspeed [[13:9|AC 61-67C p3]]. Below L/DMAX a speed loss keeps growing unless you lower the AOA or add power [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].
